Elena Duarte

gap-001 · supplement · fictional age 16

Written life first, then interpreted by a separate response author without the engine or results. These are synthetic checks. There is no correct career answer key.

Life from age 4 to 16

I like little things being right. That sounds fussy. I can leave my laundry everywhere, so apparently it only counts for some things. People say I am gentle because I am quiet, but being quiet does not mean I know what to say. I want to keep learning the tooth stuff. I do not want every adult conversation to end with a decision about my whole life.

  • family: Lives with both parents and a younger brother; an aunt nearby is a dental assistant. Family relationships are affectionate and occasionally noisy.
  • finances: Stable household income; extracurricular fees require choosing one paid activity at a time.
  • geography: El Paso, Texas; cousins live across the border and visit when arrangements permit.
  • cultureLanguages: Uses Spanish and English at home; reads recreationally mostly in English.
  • school: Large public high school; steady grades with particular patience for practical assignments.
  • accessOpportunities: Has library access, a shared home laptop, inexpensive craft supplies, and occasional public clinic education events through her aunt.
  • Age 4–5

    At four Elena spent long afternoons making tiny beds for plastic animals while her brother knocked them over. She liked the folding and taping more than the pretend conversations. Her father let her sort washers in the garage, although he stopped her taking the smallest ones into the yard.

  • Age 6–7

    In first grade she enjoyed reading aloud when she had rehearsed the page. Unplanned speaking made her cheeks hot. She and a cousin traded elaborate paper bracelets and argued about whose knots held. At home, brushing teeth was mainly a chore she tried to shorten before cartoons.

  • Age 8–9

    At eight she needed several fillings. The unfamiliar sounds frightened her, but she watched a staff member assemble a demonstration tray afterward. Her aunt showed her a large teaching model, never real patient materials. Elena wanted to know why a hard tooth could have a soft inside.

  • Age 10–11

    Between ten and eleven she remade a broken doll hinge using thread, wire, and repeated attempts. Her teacher praised the repair; Elena was more pleased that it moved evenly. She also followed videos about teeth and digestion, skipping the presenters who turned every explanation into a loud joke.

  • Age 12–13

    Braces brought soreness, complaints, and a new habit of studying her mouth in a small mirror. She became good at cleaning around awkward spaces but often postponed starting. A close friend sent dramatic treatment clips; Elena asked her to stop because she disliked the fear-based commentary and surprise blood.

  • Age 14–15

    At fourteen she helped prepare paper packets for a public oral-health event and practiced using oversized floss on a plastic model. She liked explaining one concrete step. When a small child cried, she froze and fetched her aunt. She still enjoyed the afternoon and did not want to pretend otherwise.

  • Age 16

    Now sixteen, she repairs costume jewelry for two friends and can keep her hands steady through slow, fiddly work. Her aunt says she should consider following her example. Elena likes the objects and explanations but does not know whether she would enjoy strangers being uncomfortable all day. She also wants weekends for volleyball.

Life now

  • enjoys: Fine repairs · Understanding teeth and digestion · Casual volleyball
  • avoids: Unexpected graphic clips · Being expected to calm every upset child
  • activities: Repairs inexpensive jewelry · Helps her brother organize school supplies · Occasional public education events
  • demonstratedSkills: Makes secure small joins after practice · Follows a multi-step cleaning demonstration · Notices uneven spacing
  • unfamiliarActivities: Working with real dental equipment · Extended laboratory work · Daily public-facing work
  • motivations: Making something function neatly · Understanding what is happening inside a body
  • ambitions: Wants to buy her own reliable laptop · Considering an advanced biology class
  • struggles: Delays routine chores · Loses words when someone cries · Feels family suggestions becoming expectations
  • supports: Patient aunt · Friend who respects her limits · Parents who accept changing plans
  • practicalConstraints: Shared laptop · One paid activity at a time · Parents provide most transportation

Still uncertain: Would repeated contact with upset people become easier or remain draining? · Does she enjoy biological explanations beyond familiar mouth-related examples?
